quick_revision.recall_15s: Title 1 is four Regulations. 1.1 minimum age - under 16 prohibited outright, under 18 no night work (nine hours, midnight to 5 a.m., training exception only) and no hazardous work. 1.2 medical certificate - held before starting, STCW accepted, a duly qualified practitioner, two years maximum, one year under 18, colour vision six years, and if it expires on a voyage it continues to the next port up to three months. 1.3 training - trained or certified competent, plus personal safety training, and there is NO Standard A1.3 because the Regulation defers to STCW. 1.4 recruitment and placement - no charge to the seafarer, no blacklists, licensed private services, a register, and insurance against the agent's or owner's default. Part A is mandatory, Part B is due consideration.
critical_numbers: Minimum age 16 absolute; 18 for night work and hazardous work
Night - at least nine hours, starting no later than midnight, ending no earlier than 5 a.m.
Medical certificate - two years maximum; one year under 18; colour vision six years
Expiry during a voyage, or an urgent case - not exceeding three months to the next port
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MLC 2006 Standard A1.4, paragraph 5(b) - no fees or other charges for seafarer recruitment or placement or for providing employment shall be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by the seafarer, other than the cost of the seafarer obtaining a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book and a passport or other similar personal travel document, not including, however, the cost of visas, which shall be borne by the shipowner.
quick_revision.major_trap: Inventing a Standard A1.3. There is none, and no Guideline B1.3 either - Regulation 1.3 stands alone and its paragraph 3 defers to the IMO's mandatory instruments, meaning STCW. The second trap is giving the minimum age as 18: it is 16 to work at all, with 18 the threshold for night work and hazardous work only.

understand_first: Title 1 is the Convention's door policy. Everything else in the MLC - hours, wages, accommodation, medical care - assumes a person is lawfully on board in the first place, and Title 1 is what decides that. Three of its four Regulations are tests applied to the individual: old enough, fit enough, trained enough. The fourth is different in kind, and that difference is the point of the Title. Regulating the manning agent is what stops the other three from being satisfied on paper by a crew that paid for the privilege and cannot complain about anything. If you can see why recruitment and placement belongs in the same Title as minimum age, the four notes stop being a list and become an argument.

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is built in three parts - the Articles, the Regulations, and the Code. The Code has two halves: Part A Standards, which are mandatory, and Part B Guidelines, which are not, but to which a Member must give due consideration (Article VI). Article VI.3 allows a Member to implement a Part A requirement by substantial equivalence. Title 1 is headed "Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship" and contains exactly the four Regulations this question sets, in this order.

The shape of Title 1 is worth stating before the detail: three of its four Regulations answer the question "may this particular person work at sea at all?" - age, health, competence - and the fourth regulates the system that put them on the ship. That is why recruitment and placement belongs in a Title otherwise about the individual.

blocks.h: 2. (a) Minimum age to work on a ship

blocks.p: Regulation 1.1 - purpose: to ensure that no under-age persons work on a ship. No person below the minimum age shall be employed, engaged or work on a ship. Standard A1.1 sets three separate rules, and the marks are in keeping them apart:

ul: A1.1.1 - the hard floor. The employment, engagement or work on board of any person under the age of 16 is prohibited. There is no exception to this one.

A1.1.2 - night work. Night work of seafarers under 18 is prohibited. Night is defined in accordance with national law, but must cover at least nine hours, starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m.

A1.1.3 - the only exception, and it is to the night rule alone. The competent authority may except a seafarer where effective training under an established programme would otherwise be impaired, or where the specific nature of the duty or a recognized training programme requires night duty and the authority determines, after consultation with shipowners' and seafarers' organizations, that it will not be detrimental to their health or well-being.

A1.1.4 - hazardous work. Employment of seafarers under 18 is prohibited where the work is likely to jeopardize their health or safety. The types of such work are determined by national laws or the competent authority, after tripartite consultation, in accordance with relevant international standards.

blocks.p: So there are two ages, not one: 16 is the absolute minimum for working at all, and 18 is the threshold below which night work and hazardous work are additionally restricted.

blocks.h: 3. (b) Medical certification for duties on board

blocks.p: Regulation 1.2 - seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are certified as medically fit to perform their duties; exceptions only as prescribed in the Code. Standard A1.2 supplies the detail.

ul: Held before starting. A valid medical certificate attesting fitness for the duties they are to carry out at sea must be held prior to beginning work (A1.2.1). The competent authority prescribes the nature of the examination and the certificate after tripartite consultation (A1.2.2).
STCW is accepted. A certificate issued under STCW is accepted for the purposes of Regulation 1.2, so one examination satisfies both instruments (A1.2.3).

Who issues it. A duly qualified medical practitioner, or - for a certificate concerning eyesight alone - a person recognized by the competent authority as qualified. Practitioners must enjoy full professional independence in their medical judgement (A1.2.4). In India this means a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, acting under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it.

Right of further examination. A seafarer refused a certificate, or given a limitation as to time, field of work or trading area, must be given the opportunity of a further examination by another independent practitioner or an independent medical referee (A1.2.5).

What it must state. That hearing and sight are satisfactory - and colour vision where fitness is liable to be affected by defective colour vision; and that the seafarer is not suffering from a condition likely to be aggravated by service at sea, to render him unfit, or to endanger the health of others on board (A1.2.6).

Validity. A maximum of two years; one year if the seafarer is under 18; a certification of colour vision, six years (A1.2.7). These are maxima - a shorter period may be required by the specific duties or under STCW.

Expiry at sea. If validity expires in the course of a voyage, the certificate continues in force until the next port of call where a certificate can be obtained, not exceeding three months (A1.2.9). Separately, in urgent cases, the authority may permit work without a valid certificate to the next port, again not exceeding three months, provided the seafarer holds an expired certificate of recent date (A1.2.8).
Language. For ships ordinarily engaged on international voyages the certificate must be provided as a minimum in English (A1.2.10).

blocks.p: Regulation 1.3 - purpose: to ensure that seafarers are trained or qualified to carry out their duties on board ship. This limb has a feature worth noticing and stating, because it is the one thing here a well-prepared candidate can say that others will not: there is no Standard A1.3 and no Guideline B1.3. Regulation 1.3 stands alone, without a Part A Standard beneath it. The reason is that the detailed requirements already exist elsewhere - in STCW - and the Convention deliberately does not duplicate them.

ul: Reg 1.3.1 - seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are trained or certified as competent or otherwise qualified to perform their duties.

Reg 1.3.2 - seafarers shall not be permitted to work unless they have successfully completed training for personal safety on board ship. This is the basic safety training limb, and it applies to every seafarer, not only to certificated officers.

Reg 1.3.3 - the bridge to STCW. Training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the IMO shall be considered as meeting the requirements of paragraphs 1 and 2. So an STCW certificate of competency and the STCW basic training discharge this Regulation.

Reg 1.3.4 - a transitional provision preserving obligations under the Certification of Able Seamen Convention, 1946 (No. 74) for Members bound by it, until IMO provisions covering the subject matter enter into force or five years elapse from entry into force of the MLC, whichever is earlier.

blocks.p: Regulation 1.4 - purpose: to ensure that seafarers have access to an efficient and well-regulated seafarer recruitment and placement system. All seafarers shall have access to an efficient, adequate and accountable system for finding employment on board ship without charge to the seafarer. Services operating in a Member's territory must conform to the Code; and a Member must require that shipowners using services based in countries where the Convention does not apply ensure those services conform too (Reg 1.4.3) - the provision that stops the obligation being avoided by recruiting through a non-Party State.

Standard A1.4 regulates the services. A public service must be operated in an orderly manner protecting seafarers' employment rights (A1.4.1). Private services must operate only under a standardized system of licensing or certification or other regulation, established after consultation with shipowners' and seafarers' organizations; and undue proliferation of private services shall not be encouraged (A1.4.2). A Member adopting such a system must at a minimum (A1.4.5):

ul: Prohibit blacklisting - the use of means, mechanisms or lists intended to prevent or deter seafarers from gaining employment for which they are qualified.

Prohibit fees. No fees or other charges for recruitment, placement or providing employment may be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by the seafarer - other than the cost of a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book, and a passport or similar travel document. The cost of visas is expressly excluded and is borne by the shipowner.
Require services to maintain an up-to-date register of all seafarers recruited or placed, available for inspection by the competent authority.
Require that seafarers are informed of their rights and duties before or during engagement, can examine their employment agreements before and after signing, and receive a copy.
Require services to verify that seafarers are qualified and hold the necessary documents, and that agreements accord with applicable law and any collective bargaining agreement.
Require services to make sure, as far as practicable, that the shipowner has the means to protect seafarers from being stranded in a foreign port.
Require services to examine and respond to complaints and advise the competent authority of any unresolved complaint.

Require a system of protection - insurance or an equivalent measure - to compensate seafarers for monetary loss arising from the failure of the service, or of the shipowner under the employment agreement, to meet its obligations.

blocks.p: The competent authority must closely supervise and control all such services, granting or renewing licences only after verification of compliance (A1.4.6), and must ensure machinery exists for investigating complaints about their activities (A1.4.7).

blocks.h: 6. How Title 1 is certified and enforced

blocks.p: Title 1 is not merely aspirational: its four subjects are the first four of the sixteen areas listed in Appendix A5-I which must be inspected and approved before a Maritime Labour Certificate is issued, and they are declared in the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance - Part I stating the national requirements and Part II the shipowner's measures. The certificate and DMLC are accepted by a port State as prima facie evidence of compliance (Reg 5.2.1), and the same subjects appear in Appendix A5-III as areas open to a more detailed port State inspection. On board, the practical evidence a Chief Engineer should expect to be asked for is the age and medical certificate of every engine-room rating, the STCW certificates and basic safety training of the watchkeepers, and the manning agent's licence behind the crew list.

"Write a short note on the following" with four lettered limbs is an instruction about layout as much as content. Four headings, in the printed order, lettered as printed. Roughly four marks each, so roughly equal length - and the commonest failure is to write three pages on medical certificates, because that is the limb most familiar from daily practice, and two lines on recruitment and placement. Resist it. A short framing paragraph naming Title 1 and the mandatory status of Part A is worth having, because it lets all four limbs cite Standards without re-explaining what a Standard is.

blocks.h: The idea that ties the four together

blocks.p: Title 1 answers one question in four ways: who is allowed on the ship in the first place. Age, health and competence are three tests applied to the individual - is this person old enough, fit enough, trained enough. Recruitment and placement is a test applied to the system that supplied them. The Convention's insight is that the first three are worth little if the fourth is unregulated: a manning agent that charges fees, blacklists complainers and cannot be inspected will produce crews who are nominally compliant and actually coerced. Saying that in one sentence turns four disconnected notes into an answer.

blocks.h: The detail that separates a good answer here

blocks.p: There is no Standard A1.3. Regulations 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4 each have a Part A Standard beneath them; Regulation 1.3 does not, and neither does it have a Part B Guideline. That is not an oversight - the Convention points at STCW instead, and Regulation 1.3, paragraph 3 says expressly that training and certification under the IMO's mandatory instruments shall be considered as meeting the requirement. Most candidates will invent a Standard A1.3 to keep the pattern tidy. Stating correctly that none exists, and explaining why, is worth more than a paragraph of invented content - and it demonstrates the candidate has read the instrument rather than a summary of it.

blocks.h: The two ages, and why examiners like them

blocks.p: 16 and 18 do different work. 16 is a prohibition on working at all, with no exception anywhere in the Standard. 18 is a threshold for two further restrictions - night work and hazardous work - and the night restriction is the only one carrying an exception, for training. Candidates routinely merge these into a single vague statement that "young seafarers are protected", or attach the training exception to the age-16 rule, where it does not belong. Set them out as three separate rules and the limb is secure.

ul: Inventing a Standard A1.3. It does not exist. Regulation 1.3 stands alone and points to STCW.
Saying the minimum age is 18. It is 16; 18 is the threshold for night work and hazardous work.
Attaching the training exception to the minimum age. It applies only to the night-work restriction.
Giving medical certificate validity as two years without the qualifications - one year under 18, six years for colour vision, and all of them maxima.

Confusing the two three-month provisions: A1.2.9 is a certificate expiring during a voyage, which continues in force; A1.2.8 is an urgent case where the authority permits work on a recently expired certificate. Different triggers, same ceiling.
Saying the seafarer pays nothing at all. The seafarer may bear the cost of the statutory medical certificate, the seafarer's book and a passport - but not visas, which fall on the shipowner.
Omitting Regulation 1.4.3, the provision reaching services based in non-Party States. It is the limb that makes the rest enforceable.
Forgetting the insurance or equivalent requirement in A1.4.5 - the financial protection against a manning agent's or shipowner's default.
Writing about hours of rest, wages or accommodation. Those are Titles 2 and 3 and earn nothing here.

blocks.p: "What is Standard A1.3?" - a trap question. There is none; Regulation 1.3 has no Part A Standard, and the requirement is met through STCW. "A cadet of 17 is on the 12-4 watch. Any problem?" Yes - night work under 18 is prohibited, and the watch spans the protected period; it is lawful only under the A1.1.3 training exception, granted by the competent authority after tripartite consultation. "His medical expired yesterday, mid-ocean. Must we divert?" No - A1.2.9 continues it in force to the next port of call where a certificate can be obtained, up to three months. "The manning agent deducted one month's wages as a placement fee." Prohibited outright by A1.4.5(b), directly or indirectly, in whole or in part. "Who pays for the visa?" The shipowner - the exclusion is express.

ul: Which Title of the MLC deals with minimum requirements? Title 1, and its four Regulations are 1.1 to 1.4.
Is Part B mandatory? No - Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B Guidelines must be given due consideration (Article VI).
What is substantial equivalence? Article VI.3 - a Member may implement a Part A requirement differently provided it gives effect to the general object and purpose.
How long is a medical certificate valid? Two years maximum; one year under 18; colour vision six years.
Who may issue one? A duly qualified medical practitioner - or, for eyesight alone, a person recognized by the competent authority. In India, a DG Shipping approved examiner.
What if a seafarer is refused a certificate? A1.2.5 - a further examination by another independent practitioner or an independent medical referee.
Can a manning agent charge you a fee? No. A1.4.5(b), other than the statutory medical certificate, seafarer's book and passport. Not visas.
What protects you if the manning agent goes bust owing you wages? A1.4.5(c)(vi) - a system of protection by insurance or equivalent measure to compensate monetary loss.
Where is Title 1 checked on board? Appendix A5-I, the first four of the sixteen areas, declared in the DMLC and inspected for the Maritime Labour Certificate.

blocks.p: AGE - FIT - TRAINED - SUPPLIED. Age (step 2, Reg 1.1 - 16 and 18). Fit (step 3, Reg 1.2 - two, one, six, and three months). Trained (step 4, Reg 1.3 - no Standard, see STCW). Supplied (step 5, Reg 1.4 - no fees, no blacklists, register, insurance). The first three test the person; the fourth tests the system that sent them.

ul: MLC 2006 Article VI - Regulations and Parts A and B of the Code; Part A mandatory, Part B due consideration; Article VI.3 substantial equivalence.
Regulation 1.1 and Standard A1.1 - minimum age. A1.1.1 under 16 prohibited; A1.1.2 night work under 18; A1.1.3 the training exception; A1.1.4 hazardous work under 18.

Regulation 1.2 and Standard A1.2 - medical certificate. A1.2.1 held before starting; A1.2.3 STCW accepted; A1.2.4 who issues; A1.2.5 further examination; A1.2.6 content; A1.2.7 validity; A1.2.8 urgent cases; A1.2.9 expiry during a voyage; A1.2.10 English.
Regulation 1.3 - training and qualifications. No Standard A1.3 and no Guideline B1.3 exist. Reg 1.3.3 routes to the IMO's mandatory instruments; Reg 1.3.4 the Convention No. 74 transitional.

Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4 - recruitment and placement. Reg 1.4.1 without charge; Reg 1.4.3 services in non-Party States; A1.4.2 licensing of private services; A1.4.5 the minimum content, including (a) blacklists, (b) fees, (c)(i) register, (c)(vi) insurance; A1.4.6 supervision; A1.4.7 complaints.
STCW 1978 as amended - the instrument Regulation 1.3 defers to, including basic safety training.
Appendix A5-I - the sixteen areas for inspection and certification; Appendix A5-III - areas open to port State detailed inspection; Regulation 5.2.1 - certificate and DMLC as prima facie evidence.
India: Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it; Directorate General of Shipping approves medical examiners and licenses recruitment and placement services.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the text in force

blocks.p: The amendment position at this sitting. The operative text is the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 as amended. The 2022 amendments were in force at this sitting, having entered into force in December 2024. The 2025 amendments had been adopted but were NOT in force, and nothing from them appears in this answer. Every provision quoted above is quoted from the Convention text itself.

What is not asserted. The amendments of 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022 have concentrated on Titles 2 to 5 - financial security for abandonment and for shipowners' liability, repatriation, harassment and bullying, personal protective equipment, social connectivity and the certification regime. No claim is made here that Title 1 has never been amended, because MIW's verification of the consolidated text is at Regulation and Standard level for Title 1 rather than a clause-by-clause amendment history. The Title 1 provisions above are stated as they stand in the Convention text and were correct at this sitting; a session needing the amendment history of an individual Title 1 paragraph should establish it from the amendment resolutions rather than from this record.

The Indian layer - that DG Shipping approves medical examiners and licenses recruitment and placement services under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - is carried as verified internal reuse from the QP2511 Q3 record. Note that the 1958 Act is the operative Indian statute at this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had assent but had not commenced, and is not relied on anywhere in this answer.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q1 on this paper. Q1 asks for the certificates issued to a vessel for maintaining health on board, and their validity and extension; this question asks for the certificate the seafarer holds, and its validity and extension. The shapes are deliberately parallel - a maximum period, and a limited extension to reach the next port where the document can be obtained - and the instruments are different: the International Health Regulations for the ship, MLC Standard A1.2 for the seafarer. Six months plus one for the ship; two years plus three months for the seafarer. An examiner who has set both on one paper is testing whether the candidate can tell the ship's paperwork from the crew's.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four Regulations of MLC Title 1.
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 1.1 minimum age; Regulation 1.2 medical certificate; Regulation 1.3 training and qualifications; Regulation 1.4 recruitment and placement. Three test the individual - old enough, fit enough, trained enough - and the fourth regulates the system that supplied them.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed limbs map one-to-one onto the four Regulations, in order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: MLC minimum age - which ages, and what does each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two ages. Under 16, employment, engagement or work on board is prohibited outright with no exception (A1.1.1). Under 18, night work is prohibited, night being at least nine hours starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m. (A1.1.2), and work likely to jeopardize health or safety is prohibited (A1.1.4).
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two ages into one statement is the commonest error on this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the training exception let a 15-year-old work on a ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The exception in A1.1.3 applies only to the night-work restriction for seafarers under 18, where effective training would otherwise be impaired or the duty requires it, and only after the competent authority consults shipowners' and seafarers' organizations. The prohibition on anyone under 16 working at all carries no exception.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates attach the exception to the wrong rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long is a seafarer's medical certificate valid, and what happens if it expires at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18; a certification of colour vision a maximum of six years (A1.2.7). These are maxima and a shorter period may be required by the duties or under STCW. If validity expires in the course of a voyage the certificate continues in force until the next port of call where one can be obtained, not exceeding three months (A1.2.9).
retrieval_cards.why: The qualifications carry the marks; the bare two years does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Standard A1.2 paragraph 8 from paragraph 9.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 9 covers a certificate whose validity expires during a voyage - it continues in force to the next port where a certificate can be obtained, up to three months. Paragraph 8 covers urgent cases where the seafarer is already working without a valid certificate - the competent authority may permit it to the next port, up to three months, provided the seafarer holds an expired certificate of recent date. Different triggers, same three-month ceiling.
retrieval_cards.why: Two provisions with the same number of months and different conditions.

retrieval_cards.answer: Nothing - there is no Standard A1.3, and no Guideline B1.3 either. Regulation 1.3 stands alone without a Part A Standard. Its paragraph 3 provides that training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the IMO shall be considered as meeting its requirements, so the detail lives in STCW and the Convention does not duplicate it.
retrieval_cards.why: A trap question that rewards having read the instrument rather than a summary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a seafarer never be charged for, and what may they be charged for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A1.4.5(b). No fees or other charges for recruitment, placement or providing employment may be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by the seafarer. The exceptions are the cost of a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book, and a passport or similar personal travel document. The cost of visas is expressly excluded from the exceptions and is borne by the shipowner.
retrieval_cards.why: The visa point is the detail examiners use to separate recall from reading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What protects a seafarer if the manning agent or shipowner defaults on its obligations?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A1.4.5(c)(vi) requires a system of protection, by way of insurance or an equivalent appropriate measure, to compensate seafarers for monetary loss incurred as a result of the failure of a recruitment and placement service, or of the relevant shipowner under the employment agreement, to meet its obligations to them.
retrieval_cards.why: The financial-protection limb is routinely omitted from limb (d).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does Regulation 1.4 reach a manning agent in a country that has not ratified the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 1.4 paragraph 3. Each Member must require, for seafarers working on ships flying its flag, that shipowners using recruitment and placement services based in countries or territories where the Convention does not apply ensure that those services conform to the requirements of the Code. The obligation is placed on the shipowner rather than on the foreign service.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what stops the Title being avoided by recruiting offshore.

retrieval_cards.answer: No. Under Article VI the Regulations and Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B Guidelines are not, but Members must give due consideration to implementing their Part A responsibilities in the manner provided in Part B. Article VI.3 additionally allows implementation by substantial equivalence. Port State inspection deals only with the Articles, Regulations and Part A Standards.
retrieval_cards.why: Frames every citation in the answer and is a standing oral question.
